opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Disagreement on a founding team like this is almost guaranteed, and I think that's a good thing. If everyone agrees all the time, you probably don't have enough diversity of perspective.

Researchers and industry practitioners are often optimizing for different things. Someone from research asks whether the idea is fundamentally right, whether it's elegant, whether it generalizes. Someone from industry asks whether it ships, whether customers want it, whether it scales cost-effectively. Both are legitimate, and the hard part is making sure they're actually talking about the same question.

So the first thing I try to do is separate the kinds of disagreement. Some are factual: will this training approach work, will this architecture scale? Those you can often resolve with experiments. In AI that's a big advantage, because you can build a small prototype, run an ablation, and let the data speak instead of arguing for weeks. I'm a strong believer in "let's just try it" when the cost of trying is low.

Other disagreements are about values or priorities: do we chase the long-term research bet or the near-term product? Experiments won't settle those. You need to be explicit about goals and timelines, and accept that someone has to make a call. It helps to agree up front on who owns which kind of decision, so not every disagreement becomes a debate among equals that never ends.

Another thing I've learned is to keep disagreement about ideas, not people. Strong-minded people can argue intensely and still trust each other, as long as everyone believes the others are acting in good faith for the shared mission. Once that trust erodes, even small technical disagreements become political. So I think it's worth investing early in alignment on the mission and on how you'll make decisions, before the stakes get high.

Finally, there needs to be room to be wrong. In research, most ideas fail. If someone loses an argument and the other direction turns out to be wrong, the team should be able to change course without blame. That makes people more willing to commit to a decision even when they disagree, because they know the team will revisit it honestly when new evidence comes in.

r001.rationale: The response recommends testing factual disagreements, clarifying goals, and aligning on the mission, but does not say that agreement on ideas and their underlying logic is the basis for deciding what the team pursues together.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's something I think about a lot, because when you bring together people who have spent years at places like Meta, Google, or in academia, every one of them has strong opinions backed by real experience. Disagreement is not a bug. If everyone agreed all the time, I'd be worried we weren't thinking hard enough.

The first thing I try to do is separate the type of disagreement. Some disagreements are really about facts, and those should be resolved by experiments. If someone believes one architecture will scale better than another, we don't need to argue for three hours in a meeting. We run the ablation, we look at the curves, and the data settles it. Researchers are usually quite comfortable with that, because that's how we were trained. The key is to make the experiment cheap enough and fast enough that it's actually worth running instead of debating.

The second type is disagreement about taste or direction, like which problem is worth solving, or whether we should optimize for a demo next month or a foundation that pays off in a year. Those can't be settled by an experiment, and this is where founding teams actually break. For those, I think you need two things. One is a shared understanding of what the company is ultimately trying to do, so that arguments are anchored to something bigger than any individual's preference. The other is clear ownership. Somebody has to be the decision maker for a given area, and once they decide, the rest of the team commits even if they would have chosen differently. Otherwise you get this slow erosion where every decision is relitigated.

I also think the research mindset can be a double-edged sword here. In research, being right is almost the whole game, and you're rewarded for defending your position. In a company, being right but six months late is the same as being wrong. So I try to encourage people, including myself, to be honest about how confident they really are. A lot of heated arguments dissolve when someone admits, "I'm maybe sixty percent on this," and then you realize it's not worth fighting over, just try it and see.

And finally, trust. If people trust each other's intentions, that you're arguing because you want the thing to succeed and not because of ego, then even very intense disagreements stay healthy. That trust is built in the small moments, like someone changing their mind publicly when the evidence comes in. When the team sees that happen a few times, it becomes the culture.

r001.rationale: The response says to anchor disagreements to a shared company goal and use experiments or clear ownership to resolve them. It does not describe agreement on ideas and their underlying logic as the basis for deciding what the team pursues.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to understand where the disagreement comes from. Are we disagreeing about the technical approach, the priorities of the company, or what we ultimately want to build? Those are different problems. If one person wants to pursue a long-term research breakthrough and another wants to ship a product in three months, a technical debate may never resolve the underlying difference.

For technical disagreements, I would try to turn opinions into experiments. What would we expect to see if your approach is right? What is the smallest experiment that would help us decide? Strong researchers are good at defending ideas, but in a startup, you also need to be willing to update quickly when the evidence changes.

And you need clear decision ownership. Everyone should have room to challenge a proposal, but consensus cannot be a prerequisite for every action. After a decision is made, the team needs to commit to executing it, with an understanding of when to revisit it. The important thing is that people feel their reasoning was heard, even when their preferred approach was not chosen.

r001.rationale: The response recommends experiments and clear decision ownership, but does not say that the team should base what it pursues together on agreement about ideas and their underlying logic.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to understand where the disagreement comes from. Are we disagreeing about the goal, or about how to get there? Researchers may focus on whether an idea is fundamentally interesting, while people with industry experience may focus on whether we can deliver it reliably. Both perspectives are valuable, but they can lead to very different priorities.

For technical disagreements, I like to turn opinions into experiments. What is the smallest experiment we can run that would help us distinguish between these approaches? You don’t need everyone to agree in advance if you can agree on what evidence would change your mind.

But not every decision can be settled by an experiment. Sometimes you have limited time or resources, and someone needs to make the call. So it’s important to have clear ownership. Everyone should be able to challenge a decision, but once the decision is made, the team needs to move together.

Ultimately, strong-minded people can work very well together if they trust that everyone is trying to solve the same problem. The difficult situation is when defending your own idea becomes more important than finding the right answer.

r001.rationale: The response recommends agreeing on evidence that could change minds and aligning after a decision, but does not describe agreement on the ideas and their underlying logic as the basis for deciding what the team pursues together.
